sentences.text: In the second week of September the web comes down.
Iva has seen it happen twice and it takes about three days and it is not dramatic; the sheet detaches at the top corners and hangs, and then it is on the ground, and then it is not there.

The second time she watched for it deliberately, going up every evening from the first of the month, and she still missed the actual detaching on both corners, which happened, both times, in the night.
Nobody in the village has ever seen the spider do it and nobody has ever seen her spin the new one either, which starts appearing in the last week of March.
And for about six days after it comes down, the hornbeams give it back.
It starts on the evening of the day the sheet reaches the ground and it is over by the seventh morning, and in between it is continuous.
It does not stop at night.
Iva went up at two in the morning once, at seventeen, on a bet, and it was going then at the same volume with the same wash.
You walk through and you hear voices.
They are not loud.

They are at the volume of a conversation two rooms away, and they overlap completely — hundreds of them, all at once, in no order, men and women and children and a dog and once, unmistakably, a chainsaw.
It is a wash.
There is no way to pick anything out of it.
It sounds, Iva has always thought, exactly like a school corridor at the end of a lesson, heard from a stairwell.
That is everything anybody said under those hornbeams between March and August, coming back out of the trees over six days in September, all at the same time.
Nobody in Podgora finds this alarming.
They find it a nuisance, in the way you would find a road being resurfaced a nuisance — for six days the path is unpleasant to walk and the dogs will not go up it, and then it stops.
The village has a phrase for that week.
It translates roughly as *the trees are talking* and it is used the way you would use *the leaves are down* — as a marker in the year, mildly, with no weight on it at all.
Iva's mother says it every September and has never in her life given it a second thought.
Iva asked her once whether it had ever bothered her.

Her mother said that when she was small she and her brother used to go up there and shout into it, to see if they could hear themselves come back the following year, and that they never could, and that they had got bored of it by about the age of ten.
Iva found it extremely alarming in the September she was twelve, and the reason is that in April she had said something on that path.
